title: Payment-system fees redistribute across consumers through merchant prices and rewards
source_unit: US merchant, transaction, payment-method, and modeled consumer-income incidence

denominator.unit: approximately one million Fiserv merchants; paper says this covers around one-fifth of US card payments

payment_data_surface.value: merchant-level transaction volumes, counts, and fees by card type

card_payment_coverage.unit: approximate percent of US card payments

merchant_heterogeneity.value: payment composition and interchange fees vary across merchants, sectors, sizes, and negotiated contracts

observations.method: Descriptive merchant-level settlement-data analysis with a sufficient-statistics incidence framework; paper is an NBER working paper.
observations.uncertainty: The coverage is reported as approximately one-fifth of US card payments and the incidence estimate depends on pass-through and matching assumptions. Fiserv coverage is not the same as a nationally representative household sample.
observations.subgroup: Merchants differentiated by sector, size, payment composition, and fee arrangements.
observations.counterinterpretation: Merchant sorting, negotiated fees, cash discounts, surcharges, or differences in products and customers can change who bears the cost; average fees alone do not identify incidence.

denominator.unit: US dollars per year; estimated transfer across cash/debit and credit-card users

gross_transfer.unit: billion US dollars per year from cash/debit users to credit-card users

higher_income_transfer.unit: billion US dollars per year toward households earning above $150,000

cash_user_relative_burden.unit: percent higher effective sales-tax equivalent for cash users than premium credit-card users

observations.method: Sufficient-statistics framework maps observed payment-choice and merchant-fee heterogeneity into redistribution under empirically examined pass-through assumptions.
observations.uncertainty: These are model-based incidence estimates, not observed transfers on individual bills. The paper is a working paper, and the result depends on how common prices respond to payment acceptance costs and how consumer groups are matched to merchants.
observations.subgroup: Cash/debit users, credit-card users, and households above versus below the reported $150,000 income threshold.
observations.counterinterpretation: Rewards may pay for convenience, credit, fraud protection, or other services; households may choose different merchants; and merchant pricing responses may not be uniform. The estimate does not establish household welfare loss or political response.

denominator.unit: approximately 800,000 Clover merchants; paper describes Clover as a cloud-based point-of-sale platform

cash_and_card_composition.value: cash and card payments are observed together in the Clover surface

reported_2020_processing.unit: billion US dollars in transactions processed by Clover in 2020

validation_sources.value: IRS firm-size data, BEA state GDP, industry trade journals, and the Diary of Consumer Payment Choice

observations.method: Clover transaction-data comparison and validation against public and industry sources; cash is included in this data surface unlike card-only settlement data.
observations.uncertainty: Platform merchants are not all US merchants, and the reported processing volume is context rather than a household denominator. Validation does not eliminate selection or measurement error.
observations.subgroup: Merchants and transactions observed on the Clover platform during 2019-2022.
observations.counterinterpretation: Platform composition, merchant selection, transaction recording, and cash-reporting differences may affect the measured payment mix and its comparability with national data.

related_sources.claim: Accessible explanation of the payment-rewards study and its reported transfer estimate.
Official NBER DOI metadata for Working Paper 35067.

boundary: This record promotes the underlying NBER paper beyond the prior HBS-only source note, while preserving that the central dollar figures are modeled incidence estimates. It does not establish a household-level bill, welfare effect, financial-stress outcome, or political response, and the paper remains a working paper rather than a peer-reviewed publication.
